tier_reason: The only numbers are a compile-time table in a rival library's README (ZXShady/enchantum); the source generator benchmarks/gen.py is public but the timing driver, exact command lines, library versions and CPU model are not, and the compiler versions are listed only as the author's local test setup, so it cannot be A, and a rival's README is not a well-known independent suite, so not B.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Compile time in seconds (lower is better), magic_enum vs conjure_enum, all ratios derived from page data: GCC Small 47 vs 97.1 (2.1x), Big 21 vs 81.7 (3.9x), Ideal 8.1 vs 46.8 (5.8x); Clang Small 47 vs 66.8 (1.4x), Big 18 vs 52.9 (2.9x), Ideal 8.7 vs 32 (3.7x); MSVC Big 37 vs 244.9 (6.6x), Ideal 17.9 vs 95.7 (5.3x), Small 80 vs ERROR (conjure_enum hit C1060 compiler out of heap space). Clang object size KB: Small 732 vs 779, Big 1307 vs 1400, Ideal 1051 vs 1123; Clang executable size KB: Small 95 vs 243, Big 168 vs 357, Ideal 134 vs 305. The Large Range case (-1024..1024) timed out (>20 min) for magic_enum on all three compilers (GCC, Clang and MSVC); conjure_enum was Unknown on GCC and timed out on Clang and MSVC.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: -O3 for GCC and Clang, /Ox for MSVC; the README says the library was tested locally on Windows 10 with Visual Studio 2022 (19.44), GCC 14.2.0 and Clang 20.1.2 but does not tie these versions to the benchmark runs; conjure_enum built with FIX8_CONJURE_ENUM_MINIMAL; magic_enum range set through MAGIC_ENUM_RANGE_MIN/MAX. Source generator: benchmarks/gen.py in ZXShady/enchantum (the timing driver is not published).
corrections.workload: Compile time of one generated translation unit per library and case, each calling the library's to_string once per enum: 200 small enums (16 members, reflection range -128..128), 32 big enums (200 members, -256..256), 200 enums with a large range (16 members, -1024..1024) and 100 enums with an ideal range (50 members, 0..50); each averaged over 10 runs. Object-file and executable sizes measured on Clang only.
corrections.caveats: The only numbers found are in a competitor's README (enchantum). Its purpose is to show enchantum beats magic_enum: enchantum compiles 2.7x to 8.1x faster than magic_enum in the same table (for example GCC Small 6.0 s vs 47 s), simple_enum compiles faster than magic_enum in every row except MSVC Small (186 s vs 80 s) and the Large Range rows where magic_enum timed out (GCC Small 21.5 s vs 47 s), and magic_enum's own object and executable sizes are 2.4x to 15.6x larger than enchantum's. magic_enum timed out (>20 min) on the Large Range case with every compiler. The win over conjure_enum is implicit (the README lists conjure_enum as slow to compile with bigger binaries and attributes this to storing namespace-qualified names, although conjure_enum is based on magic_enum's implementation); conjure_enum is a niche baseline, and magic_enum is better read as the incumbent that others beat. benchmarks/gen.py only generates the sources; the timing script, exact command lines, library versions and CPU are not published, and the compiler versions are given only as the author's local test setup, so this is first-party-to-a-rival, tier C. No runtime benchmark exists for magic_enum against std::string_view tables, switch statements or hand-written conversions: the repo has no benchmark directory and Magic Enum's own README claims no speed numbers.

notes: Numbers match the enchantum README exactly; corrected the Large Range timeout (magic_enum timed out on Clang too, not only GCC and MSVC), the caveat that simple_enum beats magic_enum in every row (MSVC Small is 186 s vs 80 s), and added the executable sizes where magic_enum is also smaller than conjure_enum. enchantum and simple_enum are already verified wave-4 entries that beat magic_enum in this same table; magic_enum itself is a 6.2k-star incumbent with no first-party speed claim. Metadata checked: MIT, 6.2k stars, not a fork, last commit 2026-10-05.

tier_reason: rapidyaml's published benchmark suite (bm/bm_parse.cpp, results in biojppm/rapidyaml-data) is independent of both libyaml and yaml-cpp and shows libyaml_arena 86.79 MB/s vs yamlcpp_arena 11.71 MB/s on travis.yml; the compiler (g++ 16.1, Release, C++17) appears only in the build-directory name and exact flags and the CPU model are not stated, so it stays below A.

corrections.compiler_and_flags: g++ 16.1, CMake Release build, C++17, per the build directory name linux-x86_64-gxx16.1-Release-17 in ryml-bm-parse-travis.md; exact flags not stated. Google Benchmark v1.9.5, library_build_type release. libyaml is fetched from its master branch (shallow) and yaml-cpp is pinned to commit 587b24e2eedea1afa21d79419008ca5f7bda3bf4 in bm/CMakeLists.txt. Benchmark source bm/bm_parse.cpp in https://github.com/biojppm/rapidyaml.
corrections.caveats: Independent of both libraries but not a libyaml-focused suite: the rapidyaml benchmark exists to show ryml is about 3.6x faster than libyaml on this file (about 310 MB/s vs 86.79 MB/s). libyaml here is driven through rapidyaml's own wrapper (c4::yml::LibyamlParser in bm/libyaml.hpp) that builds a ryml Tree, whereas yaml-cpp builds its own Node DOM via YAML::Load, so the output structures differ; the wrapper cannot handle anchors and references (the suite skips libyaml on trusty.yml for that reason). The result JSON names the executable ryml-bm-parse-0.15.2 although the results directory is 0.16.0-pre. Exact compiler flags are not in the result files (only the build-directory name g++ 16.1 Release C++17) and the CPU model is not named, which keeps it below tier A. Single small file for the headline row (the README adds scatter plots over many files whose raw table was not read). The compile_commands.json row (135.06 vs 22.53 MB/s, 6.00x) comes from the README's JSON performance table, where libfyaml is faster than libyaml (149.15 MB/s). yaml-cpp is a widely known slow baseline and is pinned to an older fixed commit while libyaml is built from master.

notes: All claimed numbers match ryml-bm-parse-travis.txt (86.79 vs 11.71 MB/s, 7.41x; 0.05 vs 0.35 ms) and the rapidyaml README JSON table (135.06 vs 22.53 MB/s, 6.00x); hardware matches the result JSON context (20 CPUs at 4279 MHz, scaling and ASLR off, dated 2026-07-07). Added the compiler found in the result .md build path and the library pins from bm/CMakeLists.txt. Metadata checked: MIT, 1.2k stars, not archived, last commit 2026-08-21; the PyYAML CSafeLoader record already folds into this entry.
